text:
November 29, 2001
IN THE MATTER OF : Docket No. D 2002-5
RICHARD BLINCOE ET AL., : (IBLA 2001-389 et al.)

BUREAU OF LAND MANAGEMENT, :

ORDER
By petition dated October 31, 2001, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) has
requested that the Director, Office of Hearings and Appeals (OHA), assume jurisdiction of these
cases pursuant to 43 CFR 4.5(b) and review the October 24, 2001, order of the Interior Board of
Land Appeals (IBLA) granting a stay of BLM’s September 7, 2001, final grazing decisions
issued to the appellant-permittees.1/ BLM argues that IBLA committed “clear legal error” in
granting the stay sought by appellants (Petition at 11) and that the stay “causes great harm to
BLM’s ability to take measures required under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and a court-
approved settlement to protect the endangered [sic] desert tortoise” (Id. at 1-2).2/
1/ The County of San Bernardino, California, is also an appellant in these cases and had
likewise sought a stay of BLM’s September 7 decisions.
2/ The Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) has listed the Mojave population of the desert
tortoise as a threatened, not an endangered, species. 55 FR 12178 (1990). See Blincoe v. Bureau
of Land Management, No. CA-690-01-01 (OHA Hearings Division, Aug. 24, 2001) (hereinafter
“ALJ Decision”) at 7. The distinction is not significant for purposes of this litigation.
20 OHA 63A

D 2002-5
By notice and order dated November 3, 2001, I denied BLM’s petition as to most of the
appellant-permittees and gave the parties until November 13, 2001, to submit any additional
arguments, supporting declarations, and/or documents they might have on the issue of whether I
should assume jurisdiction of the cases involving the remaining appellant-permittees. Responses
were received from BLM and from appellants Richard Blincoe and Dave Fisher. For the reasons
set forth below, I hereby grant BLM’s petition in part and vacate IBLA’s October 24 stay
decision in part.
Facts and Procedural Background3/
In March 2000, the Center for Biological Diversity and other plaintiffs (the Center) filed
suit against BLM, alleging that BLM had failed to consult with FWS regarding the cumulative
effects on federally listed species of all actions authorized by BLM’s California Desert
Conservation Area (CDCA) Plan, in violation of § 7(a)(2) of the ESA,16 U.S.C. § 1536(a)(2).
Center for Biological Diversity v. Bureau of Land Management, No. C 00-00927 WHA (N.D.
Cal.). The Center further alleged that BLM was violating the ESA by allowing those activities,
including livestock grazing, to continue in the absence of consultation with FWS, citing Pacific
Rivers v. Thomas, 30 F.3d 1050 (9th Cir. 1994). As relief, the Center sought an injunction
against all activities authorized under the CDCA Plan and an order directing BLM to initiate and
complete consultation on the programmatic effects of the CDCA Plan on all federally listed
species.
The Department of Justice (DOJ), in consultation with BLM, decided to negotiate a
settlement of the case because BLM had not, in fact, consulted with FWS at the land use plan
level regarding the cumulative effects of all the activities authorized by the CDCA Plan but,
rather, had only engaged in a series of programmatic-level consultations regarding the isolated
effects of selected activities. It appeared likely to DOJ and BLM, in light of the Pacific Rivers
case, that if the matter were litigated, all activities authorized under the CDCA Plan would be
enjoined for BLM’s failure to consult on the cumulative effects of all authorized activities.
Eventually, the Center and BLM executed a total of five court-approved stipulations requiring
BLM to take various actions regarding a wide range of activities authorized under the CDCA
Plan in order to protect the desert tortoise and other listed species.
Stipulation 3, approved by the court on January 29, 2001, addressed livestock grazing
activities in desert tortoise habitat. Among other things, it provided for the seasonal exclusion of
cattle from a portion of the public lands identified as desert tortoise habitat within each of 11
grazing allotments, including appellants’, from March 1 to June 15 and from September 7 to
3/ This summary of the facts and procedural background of the case is taken largely from
the August 24 ALJ Decision at 6-19 and the October 24 IBLA Stay Decision at 1-3.
20 OHA 63B

D 2002-5
November 7 each year. Stipulation 3 specified the acreage of desert tortoise habitat to be
included in each exclusion area but not the precise location.
On April 9, 2001, BLM issued an Environmental Assessment (EA), evaluating a proposal
to temporarily modify existing livestock grazing permits in accordance with Stipulation 3.
Significantly, the EA contained an evaluation of 42 allotments to determine whether conditions
warranted emergency action pursuant to 43 CFR 4110.3-3(b). The EA concluded
that conditions, while serious, do not constitute an emergency at this time. Continued
grazing does not pose an “imminent likelihood of significant resource damage” to soils,
wildlife habitat, vegetation, and other critical values in the 42 allotments. The BLM has
been actively involved in modification of grazing practices since 1991 that has led to
improved conditions for the desert tortoise and its habitat over many [of] these
allotments. The proposed action would be an additional step to alleviate resource damage
from continued livestock grazing.
EA at 87.
On May 15, 2001, BLM issued a decision record approving the proposed action of the
EA. On the same day, BLM issued final grazing decisions to the appellant-permittees and others,
modifying the terms of their grazing permits. The final grazing decisions excluded cattle from
identified areas of desert tortoise habitat on each of 11 allotments during the spring and fall
exclusion periods; reduced the annual amount of permitted cattle use for several of the
allotments, capping it at the average number of animal unit months (AUMs) actually used for the
1997, 1998, and 1999 billing years; and imposed other restrictions to protect certain riparian
habitat areas.
Consistent with Stipulation 3, the final grazing decisions provided that
[i]f during the periods of exclusion cattle are found in the exclusion areas you will
have 48 hours after notification to remove them. If they are not removed within 48 hours,
trespass action according to 43 CFR § 4150.2(a), (b) will be taken and an additional day
will be added onto the exclusion period for every day they remain in trespass.
September 7 Decisions at 5.
BLM explained in both the decision record and final grazing decisions that it had agreed
to a settlement in the Center for Biological Diversity lawsuit “[i]n order to comply with the ESA,
as well as to preclude the potential for a desert wide injunction” against the “wide and varied”
uses of desert land authorized in the CDCA Plan. Decision Record at 5.
20 OHA 63C

D 2002-5
These interim agreements allowed BLM to continue appropriate levels of activity
throughout the planning area during the lengthy consultation process while providing
protection to the desert tortoise and other listed species in the short term. By taking
interim actions as allowed under 43 CFR Part 4100, BLM contributes to the conservation
of the endangered and threatened species in accordance with [§] 7(a)(1) of the ESA.
BLM also avoids making any irreversible or irretrievable commitment of resources which
would foreclose any reasonable and prudent alternatives which might be required as a
result of the consultation on the CDCA Plan in accordance with [§] 7(d) [of] the ESA.
* * * * * * *
The BLM’s decision is a temporary modification to current livestock grazing
administration pending completion of a Biological Opinion on the affects of the CDCA
Plan and implementation of any applicable requirements.
The BLM’s decision will provide the highest level of protection for the desert
tortoise and its habitat of any option analyzed in the EA. The cumulative impact of
reducing sheep and cattle grazing on 42 allotments will result in a slight improvement in
the existing resource conditions for the tortoise and other listed and sensitive species until
the Biological Opinion is prepared and BLM can review and implement its requirements.
Id. at 4-6.
Appellants challenged the May 15 final grazing decisions in notices of appeal filed on
June 13 and 15, 2001. By memoranda dated June 15 and 18, 2001, the Secretary assumed
jurisdiction of the appeals pursuant to 43 CFR 4.5(a) and assigned the cases to Administrative
Law Judge (ALJ) Harvey C. Sweitzer for hearing and issuance of a decision. Under a special
delegation of authority set forth in each memorandum, the Secretary provided that Judge
Sweitzer’s decisions in the cases would be final for the Department. The cases were
consolidated for a hearing, which was held in late July and early August 2001.
On August 24, 2001, Judge Sweitzer issued a 103-page decision, in which he reached the
following conclusions of law:
(1) The EA and Decision Record are legally sufficient under NEPA [the National
Environmental Policy Act];
(2) The final grazing decisions are not arbitrary and capricious, are not an abuse of
discretion, are supported upon a rational basis, and are otherwise in accordance with the
law, except as provided in conclusion (4) below;
(3) The final grazing decisions are consistent with section 7 of the ESA; and
20 OHA 63D

D 2002-5
(4) BLM complied with the grazing regulations when it issued the final grazing decisions,
except that BLM failed to comply with the requirement of consultation, cooperation, and
coordination [CCC] with the affected permittees and therefore the final grazing decisions
are hereby set aside and the matters remanded to BLM for further action consistent with
this Decision.
ALJ Decision at 103.
With respect to his fourth conclusion, Judge Sweitzer analyzed in detail the CCC
requirement as found in 43 CFR 4110.0-5 and 4.110.3-3(a), the applicable IBLA precedent, and
the extent of BLM’s communications with the appellant-permittees prior to its issuance of the
final grazing decisions. In finding that BLM had failed in its CCC obligations, Judge Sweitzer
concluded, “Consultation is an important component of an informed and rational decision
making process. Appellants should be afforded a real opportunity to contribute information and
shape the actions to be taken for the mutual benefit of all parties and the affected resources.” Id.
In response to Judge Sweitzer’s decision, BLM sent a letter to each of the appellants on
August 31, 2001, inviting them to “participate in a consultation, cooperation, and coordination
workshop regarding implementation of the court-approved Settlement Stipulations at issue in this
matter.” The workshop was scheduled for September 6-7, 2001. BLM stated that the purpose of
the workshop was to seek appellants’ “advice and exchange views on relevant issues and
proposed management actions relevant” to the final grazing decisions. BLM advised appellants
that, after fulfilling the requirements for CCC, “it is the BLM’s intent to issue revised grazing
decisions.” Appellants were asked to let BLM know, if they could not attend the workshop,
when they could meet; they were also told they could submit written advice and comment.
Similar letters were sent to the County and members of the interested public; and BLM states that
it followed up with telephone calls to the permittees, the State, and the County.
From August 28 through September 6, counsel for the respective parties engaged in
telephone conversations and exchanged correspondence over the timing and purpose of the
proposed CCC workshop. Counsel for BLM invited counsel for the permittees to submit
proposed modifications to the grazing decisions, and if any of the permittees were unable to
attend the workshop, to provide their recommendations “for adjusting the exclusion boundaries
and outlining their particular concerns so that we may discuss and address them.” After checking
with her clients, counsel for the permittees responded that “the vast majority” were unable to
meet on September 6-7, but proposed alternative meeting dates of September 13-14 or the first
week in October. Counsel for BLM responded that the meeting would take place on
September 6-7 and made reference to a “suggested conference call”; counsel further stated that
BLM intended to issue grazing decisions that would be immediately effective on September 7.
Counsel for the permittees replied that they would be unable to attend the proposed meeting on
20 OHA 63E

D 2002-5
September 6-7, but she reiterated the permittees’ offer to meet one week later and submit written
and oral comments at that time.4/
On September 5, the County responded to BLM’s August 31 invitation to the
September 6-7 CCC workshop. The County said that BLM’s letter had just arrived the day
before and that “it is impossible for the County to provide its input on such short notice * * *.”
The County assured BLM that it wanted to participate in the consultation process and requested
that the workshop be postponed to a date that would allow all the parties “an opportunity to
prepare a meaningful presentation.” Evidently the County did send two representatives to the
September 6 session with BLM, but no other interested parties appeared.
On September 7, 2001, BLM issued new, immediately effective final grazing decisions to
the appellant-permittees. The decisions recounted the procedural history of the case and cited at
length the evidence presented at the July-August hearing concerning the continuing decline of the
desert tortoise. BLM also detailed its attempts at CCC following Judge Sweitzer’s August 24
decision. The decisions explained BLM’s rationale as follows:
The imminent likelihood of significant resource damage for desert tortoise and its
habitat as determined by the hearing record and reflected in Judge Sweitzer’s decision,
caused the BLM to make this decision immediately effective to meet the fall closure date,
which begins September 7. The BLM made reasonable attempts at CCC within the
constraints of the immediacy of the fall grazing season and the requirement of the
settlement agreement that grazing not be authorized from September 7 through
November 7. Because the fall and spring closures are of critical importance to desert
tortoise biology and because cattle grazing impacts desert tortoise and its habitat, BLM
determined that this decision should be immediately effective.
September 7 Decisions at 6. In other respects, the September 7 decisions were identical to the
May 15 decisions, imposing the same modified terms and conditions on the permittees’ grazing
use.
On September 10, 2001, appellant-permittees filed notices of appeal and requests for a
stay, challenging BLM’s September 7 final grazing decisions. The County of San Bernardino
filed similar notices of appeal and stay requests on September 12. Among other things,
appellants argued that there was no change in rangeland conditions between May 15 and
September 7 that justified BLM’s issuance of immediately effective decisions; that there was still
no “imminent likelihood of significant resource damage,” as BLM had concluded in its April 9
4/ That offer was withdrawn after BLM issued the September 7 decisions.
20 OHA 63F

D 2002-5
EA; and that BLM had failed to meet its obligations for CCC as required by regulation and Judge
Sweitzer’s August 24 decision.
Pursuant to 43 CFR 4.21 and 4160.4, the cases were forwarded to IBLA for consideration
of appellants’ stay requests. BLM filed its opposition to those requests on September 21, 2001.
By order dated October 24, 2001, IBLA granted appellants’ requests for a stay of BLM’s
September 7 decisions:
We have considered the competing arguments as to whether the permittees have
met their burden of proof that the stays should be granted under 43 CFR 4.21(b). We are
mindful [of] the history of these cases, including the fact that the series of settlement
agreements reached during the [Center] for Biological Diversity litigation, particularly
Stipulation 3, dictates the course of BLM’s action to a great degree. However, we are
also cognizant, as was Judge Sweitzer, of the importance placed upon CCC by this
Department. Whether BLM’s September 7 decisions were issued following meaningful
CCC is at the heart of this dispute.
Based upon our review of the record * * *, we cannot determine whether BLM
afforded appellants a real opportunity to contribute information and shape the actions
leading to the issuance of the September 7 decisions. Since Judge Sweitzer is required to
conduct a hearing to resolve the appeals over which he has jurisdiction, i.e., to determine
whether BLM met the CCC requirement, we deem it appropriate to grant the petitions for
stay pending his ruling on the merits of whether BLM afforded permittees the “real
opportunity” to participate which he contemplated.
IBLA Stay Decision at 10-11.
As noted at the outset, on October 31, BLM filed a petition asking me to assume
jurisdiction of these cases under 43 CFR 4.5(b) and to vacate IBLA’s stay decision. BLM argued
that IBLA had failed to apply the stay criteria set forth in 43 CFR 4.21(b) and had ignored the
findings and conclusions reached by Judge Sweitzer in his August 24 decision.
On November 2, 2001, I conducted a telephonic hearing with counsel for the parties.
Since the fall 2001 exclusion period was due to end on November 7, I wanted to hear from the
parties (among other things) whether any meaningful relief could be granted in the few days
remaining, even if BLM were to convince me that IBLA had erred in granting the stay. The
parties agreed that most of the appellant-permittees had substantially complied with BLM’s
September 7 decisions with respect to the fall 2001 exclusion period. BLM expressed concern,
however, that IBLA’s stay decision authorized those permittees to return their livestock to the
exclusion areas during the remainder of the fall 2001 exclusion period and potentially to retain
20 OHA 63G

D 2002-5
their livestock in the exclusion areas during the spring 2002 exclusion period, if there were no
intervening decision on the merits of the appeals.
The parties also agreed that some appellant-permittees had not complied with the
September 7 decisions – due to impossibility, according to appellants – and that BLM had issued
trespass notices to those permittees. BLM argued that IBLA’s stay decision prevented BLM
from enforcing its trespass notices and authorized those permittees to retain their livestock in the
exclusion areas both during the remainder of the fall 2001 exclusion period and potentially
during the spring 2002 exclusion period. BLM urged me to vacate IBLA’s stay decision so that
BLM could enforce its trespass notices and the two annual closure periods. Appellants, on the
other hand, argued that the IBLA stay decision was proper and that extending the fall 2001
exclusion period past November 7 would serve no purpose other than to punish appellants.
By notice and order dated November 3, 2001, I denied BLM’s petition to assume
jurisdiction and vacate the October 24 stay as to those appellant-permittees with no outstanding
trespass notices. I observed that, with respect to those permittees, the stay issue would
essentially become moot in 4 days, at least until March 2002. I indicated that the denial of
BLM’s petition as to those permittees was without prejudice to BLM’s refiling it if there were no
decision on the merits of the appeals by the end of January 2002.
With respect to the remaining appellant-permittees, I observed that the stay issue would
apparently not become moot on November 7, given the outstanding trespass notices. The parties
were given 10 days to submit additional arguments and supporting materials on the issues of
whether I should assume jurisdiction of the cases involving the remaining appellant-permittees; if
so, whether IBLA’s October 24 stay decision should be vacated; and what effect vacating the stay
decision would have (the mootness issue).
In its November 13, 2001, response, BLM states that
the permittees with outstanding trespass notices are Dave Fisher, who has been issued a
notice of intent to impound, and William Mitchell, who has been issued a notice of
trespass. The other permittees who were issued trespass notices or letters resolved their
issues prior to the issuance of the stay on October 24, 2001. * * *
If the IBLA had not granted the stay, appellants Fisher and Mitchell would have
faced additional closure days added to the end of the fall seasonal closure. This
additional day provision is a requirement of the September 7, 2001, grazing decisions
* * * .
20 OHA 63H

D 2002-5
BLM Response at 4.5/
Given the outstanding notices issued to appellants Fisher and Mitchell, and given the
provision in the September 7 final grazing decisions for extending the seasonal exclusion period
for every day cattle were found in the permittee’s exclusion area, BLM’s petition to vacate the
stay is not moot as to these appellants, even as to the fall 2001 exclusion period. I therefore turn
to the merits of the petition.
Exercise of Discretion under 43 CFR 4.5(b)
As stated in my November 3 notice and order, the granting of a petition for review under
43 CFR 4.5(b) is within the discretionary authority of the Director. There is no right to such
review, and the Director’s review authority is exercised sparingly.
5/ Based on the discussion during the Nov. 2 telephonic hearing, I was under the impression
that the two permittees with outstanding trespass notices were Richard Blincoe and Dave Fisher,
and I indicated as much in a footnote to my Nov. 3 notice and order. Appellants’ Nov. 12
response discussed those two permittees and did not mention William Mitchell, while BLM’s
Nov. 13 response discussed appellants Fisher and Mitchell and did not mention appellant
Blincoe. On Nov. 19, 2001, appellants filed a motion to strike BLM’s arguments concerning
William Mitchell or, in the alternative, for leave to file a response on his behalf. Appellants filed
an additional motion to refer BLM’s petition to an administrative law judge for an evidentiary
hearing on the factual issues concerning the alleged trespasses. Appellants’ motions are denied.
My Nov. 3 notice and order invited the parties’ submissions concerning “the remaining
appellant-permittees – those with outstanding trespass notices.” Order at 4. The footnote stated,
“Based on the information provided during the November 2 telephonic hearing, this category
may be limited to two appellant-permittees, Richard Blincoe and Dave Fisher.” Id. Appellants
and BLM presumably had equal access to the information concerning which permittees had
outstanding trespass notices (unlike the Director). Moreover, appellants did not submit any
additional declarations or supporting documents on behalf of appellants Blincoe and Fisher,
relying instead on their declarations and supporting documents already in the record and the
additional legal arguments contained in appellants’ Nov. 12 response. I have reviewed the
declarations and other documents already in the record for appellant Mitchell, as well as
appellants’ Nov. 12 legal arguments. Consequently, appellant Mitchell has not been prejudiced
by his not being included by name in appellants’ response.
Finally, the validity of the BLM trespass notices issued to appellants Fisher and Mitchell
is not at issue in this proceeding before me. The fact that the trespass notices remain outstanding
is sufficient to establish that the relief BLM seeks is not moot, which was the issue I had raised.
Appellants may still assert whatever defenses they may have to the trespass notices if and when
BLM seeks to enforce them.
20 OHA 63I

D 2002-5
Appellant-permittees’ November 12 response argues that the Director should not assume
jurisdiction over this matter because to do so would improperly create a new opportunity for
BLM to appeal both Judge Sweitzer’s August 24 decision and IBLA’s October 24 stay.
Appellants cite the preamble to OHA’s 1985 rulemaking amending 43 CFR 4.5 for the
proposition that “the ability of the Director to review an OHA decision ‘does not modify existing
policy with respect to finality of OHA decisions for the purposes of exhaustion of administrative
remedies or create an opportunity to appeal . . . .’ 50 F.R. at 43704.” Appellants’ Response
at 7-8.
I agree that it would be improper to afford BLM an opportunity to appeal Judge
Sweitzer’s decision to the Director, since that decision was issued under a special delegation of
authority from the Secretary to render a final decision for the Department. But appellants are
mistaken in asserting that it would be improper to afford BLM an opportunity to seek
discretionary review of IBLA’s stay decision. The preamble language partially quoted by
appellants says merely that “[t]his amendment does not modify existing policy * * * or create an
opportunity for appeal to the Secretary or the Director.” 50 FR 43703-4 (emphasis added). The
1985 rulemaking amended § 4.5 to clarify that neither the Secretary nor the Director has the
authority to review a decision rendered by the Interior Board of Contract Appeals under the
Contract Disputes Act, since appeals under that Act go to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the
Federal Circuit. But nothing in § 4.5(b) prevents a party who is dissatisfied with any other
decision of an OHA appeals board from seeking discretionary review by the Director.
I have decided to grant BLM’s petition for review as to appellants Fisher and Mitchell
because of the importance of the issues raised to the parties, to grazing operations and potentially
other activities authorized in the CDCA, and to BLM’s compliance with the settlement
agreement in the Center for Biological Diversity litigation. Having analyzed the facts of this case
in relation to the stay criteria set forth in 43 CFR 4.21(b), I am unable to sustain IBLA’s October
24 decision.
Stay Criteria under 43 CFR 4.21(b)
In deciding whether to grant or deny a request for a stay, a board or the Director must
consider the four factors set forth in 43 CFR 4.21(b)(1):
(i) The relative harm to the parties if the stay is granted or denied,
(ii) The likelihood of the appellant’s success on the merits,
(iii) The likelihood of immediate and irreparable harm if the stay is not granted, and
(iv) Whether the public interest favors granting the stay[.]
Under § 4.21(b)(2), an appellant requesting a stay has the burden of proof that a stay should be
granted. As explained in the 1993 preamble to § 4.21, “the burden is on the appellant to
20 OHA 63J

D 2002-5
demonstrate in the petition for a stay that a stay is necessary under each of the criteria.” 58 FR
4939, 4941 (1993). Nevertheless, the four-part test “is not a wooden one, for * * * relief may be
granted with either a high probability of success and some injury, or vice versa.” Natural
Resources Defense Council v. E.P.A., 806 F. Supp. 275, 277 (D.D.C. 1992), quoted in Oregon
Natural Desert Ass’n, 135 IBLA 389, 393 (1996). In Jan Wroncy, 124 IBLA 150, 152-53 (1992),
IBLA discussed the interplay among the stay criteria as follows:
In balancing the movant’s likelihood of success on the merits against the potential
impact of an injunction on the parties, we have also noted that the appellant’s probability
of prevailing on the merits need not be free from doubt to justify at least an interim stay:
To justify a temporary injunction it is not necessary that the plaintiff’s
right to a final decision, after a trial, be absolutely certain, wholly without doubt;
if the other elements are present (i.e., the balance of hardships tips decidedly
toward plaintiff), it will ordinarily be enough that the plaintiff has raised questions
going to the merits so serious, substantial, difficult and doubtful, as to make them
a fair ground for litigation and thus for more deliberative investigation.
Hamilton Watch Co. v. Benrus Watch Co., 206 F.2d 738, 740 (2d Cir. 1953), quoted in
Marathon Oil Co., 90 IBLA [236, 246 (1986)].
(Emphasis added.) With these general principles in mind, I now turn to the application of the
four stay criteria to the facts of this case, although they will be discussed in a different order from
that in § 4.21(b)(1).
Likelihood of Appellants’ Success on the Merits
In his August 24 decision, Judge Sweitzer concluded that BLM’s actions in issuing the
May 15 final grazing decisions were consistent with NEPA, the ESA, the Administrative
Procedure Act (APA), and the Taylor Grazing Act and its implementing regulations, except with
respect to the CCC requirement. Since Judge Sweitzer’s decision was final for the Department,
those conclusions of law are binding on BLM, IBLA, and the Director.6/ In most respects,
BLM’s September 7 final grazing decisions are substantively identical to the May 15 final
grazing decisions, and they were issued on the basis of the same EA and decision record. At
least within the Department, therefore, appellants are unlikely to prevail on the merits of their
6/ BLM suggests that they are binding on appellants as well, since appellants did not appeal
Judge Sweitzer’s decision to federal court. BLM Response at 3. But of course appellants were
the prevailing parties in the litigation before Judge Sweitzer, so there was no adverse decision for
them to appeal.
20 OHA 63K

D 2002-5
challenges to the September 7 decisions based on NEPA, the ESA, the APA, and the non-CCC
requirements of the Taylor Grazing Act and its implementing regulations.
In one key respect, however, the September 7 final grazing decisions were a marked
departure from their May 15 counterparts. Citing an “imminent likelihood of significant resource
damage,” BLM made the September 7 decisions immediately effective. As explained in BLM’s
October 31 petition,
BLM issued the May 15 decisions under 43 CFR 4110.3-3(a) (hereinafter
“Subsection (a) decisions”). Subsection (a) decisions require “consultation, cooperation,
and coordination with the affected permittee, the State having lands or managing
resources within the area, and the interested public” before reductions in permitted
grazing use can be implemented. Subsection (a) decisions do not require findings that
resources need protection or of the imminent likelihood of significant resource damage.
Lastly, Subsection (a) decisions do not go into effect pending appeal. Compare 43 C.F.R.
§ 4.110-3.3(a) with 43 C.F.R. § 4.110-3.3(b).
BLM issued the September 7 decisions under 43 C.F.R. § 4.110-3.3(b)
(hereinafter “Subsection (b) decisions”). Subsection (b) decisions require findings that
resources need immediate protection due to conditions such as drought, fire, flood, or
insect infestation, or that continued grazing use “poses an imminent likelihood of
significant resource damage.” Subsection (b) decisions do not require consultation,
cooperation and coordination with affected permittees, but only a “reasonable attempt to
consult with, affected permittees . . . .” Subsection (b) decisions are effective upon
issuance and remain in effect pending appeal, unless stayed.
BLM made an important and intentional choice to issue the September 7 decisions
under Subsection (b).
Petition at 8.
Appellants, of course, take issue with BLM’s choice to proceed in this manner:
There are two important considerations regarding the BLM’s attempt to “ignore”
Judge Sweitzer’s August 24, 2001 ruling. The parties agree that Judge Sweitzer’s
August 24, 2001 ruling constitutes the final decision for the Department of the Interior,
pursuant to a delegation of authority by the Secretary of the Interior. * * * As indicated in
the letters issued regarding the “workshop” to the permittees, the BLM fully intended to
comply with Judge Sweitzer’s final ruling. However, sometime prior to issuance of the
final decision, the BLM changed its mind and simply issued new decisions without
compliance with Judge Sweitzer’s decision.
20 OHA 63L

D 2002-5
Appellants’ Response at 8 (emphasis in original). Or to put it another way, if Judge Sweitzer’s
rulings on the non-CCC issues in the case are final for the Department and binding on BLM, why
isn’t Judge Sweitzer’s ruling on the CCC issue likewise final and binding on BLM? Judge
Sweitzer said that “Appellants should be afforded a real opportunity to contribute information
and shape the actions to be taken for the mutual benefit of all parties and the affected resources,”
ALJ Decision at 103; yet appellants argue that they were never afforded that opportunity. The
IBLA’s stay decision reflects the same concern over whether BLM complied with Judge
Sweitzer’s ruling on CCC.
BLM’s answer to this objection is that the September 7 decisions were not intended “to
address directly the deficiencies in consultation, cooperation and coordination with permittees
identified in Judge Sweitzer’s August 24 decision.” Rather, they were “entirely new decisions
based on different regulatory authority than the May 15, 2001 decisions reviewed by Judge
Sweitzer.” Petition at 7-8.
On this point, I believe BLM has the better of the arguments, although this is obviously a
key threshold issue that Judge Sweitzer will need to decide on the merits of these appeals. Given
the August 24 decision, BLM could not have simply reissued the May 15 grazing decisions under
43 CFR 4110.3-3(a) without affording appellants the full CCC required by the regulations and
IBLA precedent. But BLM may well be right that Judge Sweitzer’s decision did not preclude
BLM from issuing new decisions under § 4110.3-3(b), assuming the conditions set forth in that
regulation were met. Indeed, in BLM’s view, Judge Sweitzer’s findings on the severity of harm
to the desert tortoise compelled their taking a different approach from that taken in May. I tend
to agree, and therefore conclude that appellants are unlikely to prevail on the merits of this
threshold issue.
But even if Judge Sweitzer’s decision did not limit BLM to proceeding only under
§ 4110.3-3(a), there is still the question of whether BLM met the requirements for proceeding
under § 4110.3-3(b). Specifically, at the time the September 7 decisions were issued, did BLM
reasonably determine that there was “an imminent likelihood of significant resource damage”
within the meaning of § 4110.3-3(b), and if so, did BLM make at least a reasonable attempt to
consult with the permittees and others prior to issuing the decisions, as required by
§ 4110.3-3(b)?
On the first of these questions, appellants argue that BLM “does not offer ONE shred of
biological evidence indicating a change in biological circumstances between the BLM’s original
May 15, 2001 decision[s] and the September 7, 2001 decision[s].” Appellants’ Response at 12
(emphasis in original). While that may be true, BLM’s September 7 decisions clearly reflect a
changed perspective on the “biological circumstances” of the allotments, as a result of the
testimony at the hearing and Judge Sweitzer’s August 24 decision. According to BLM, “Judge
Sweitzer made the finding of resource damage in his August 24, 2001 decision,” a finding that

In short, Judge Sweitzer’s detailed findings and conclusions amply demonstrate “the
criticality of the spring and fall seasons to the tortoise and the likely effects of grazing on the
tortoise during those seasons” (Id. at 90). Thus it appears likely that, at the trial on the merits,
BLM will be able to establish that urgent action was needed following Judge Sweitzer’s decision
and that BLM was therefore justified in issuing its September 7 decisions under 43 CFR
4110.3-3(b).
Finally, even if BLM was not required to engage in the full CCC required by 43 CFR
4110.3-3(a), there is still the question of whether BLM made “a reasonable attempt to consult”
with the permittees and others as required by § 4110.3-3(b). In its September 20 opposition to
appellants’ stay requests, BLM argues that it had done so:
The Bureau invited each Appellant, and counsel, as well as the County * * * to a CCC
workshop to be held on September 6 and 7, 2001, in Barstow, California * * *. For
reasons not fully explained, none of the Appellants attended the workshop * * *. None of
the Appellants participated in a conference call offered to Appellants through their
counsel, nor did any Appellant submit any written documentation evidencing their
concerns with the restrictions identified in the May 15, 2001, final grazing decisions.
Opposition at 2-3. In light of the imminence of the fall exclusion period and its importance to
the desert tortoise, BLM maintains, its efforts to consult with appellants were reasonable.
Appellants counter that they were unable to attend BLM’s CCC workshop on such short
notice, that they were not in fact offered a conference call with BLM, that providing advance
comments to BLM for use in a meeting they were unable to attend would not have constituted
true consultation, and that they had offered to meet with BLM a mere week later for a meaningful
exchange of views. While appellants couch their arguments in terms of the full CCC
requirement of § 4110.3-3(a), the same points raise legitimate issues as to the reasonableness of
BLM’s efforts at consultation under § 4110.3-3(b). Even accepting BLM’s argument about the
importance of the fall exclusion period to the desert tortoise, one still wonders whether a
“reasonable attempt to consult” with appellants would not have countenanced a single week’s
delay under the circumstances.
At a minimum, therefore, I believe that appellants have “raised questions going to the
merits” of the consultation issue “so serious, substantial, difficult and doubtful, as to make them
a fair ground for litigation and thus for more deliberative investigation.” Hamilton Watch Co.,
206 F.2d at 740. Thus, if “the balance of hardships [tipped] decidedly toward” appellants (id.)
and the other criteria in 43 CFR 4.21(b)(1) were met, I would affirm IBLA’s stay decision.

Judge Sweitzer’s decision concluded that, while the harm caused to appellants
individually should not be minimized, it was not significant to the overall regional economy.
Moreover, “under the grazing regulations, ‘even severe economic injury to a grazer does not
invalidate [a] BLM[] decision, but is only one consideration bearing on the reasonableness of that
determination. If BLM's decision has a reasonable basis, it must be affirmed.’ Yardley, 123
IBLA [80,] 93 [(1992)].” ALJ Decision at 96. But Judge Sweitzer was deciding the merits of
BLM’s May 15 final grazing decisions, not the issue of immediate and irreparable harm to
appellants for purposes of a stay request. As the quotation from Yardley suggests, a showing of
harm may be sufficient to justify a temporary stay, if the other criteria in 43 CFR 4.21(b)(1) are
also met, and yet be insufficient to invalidate BLM’s decision on the merits, if the decision has a
reasonable basis.
Thus it appears likely in this case that (a) appellants will suffer at least some significant
economic injury from implementation of the September 7 grazing decisions and may even be
forced out of business, (b) such injury will be immediate in that BLM is poised to enforce the
September 7 decisions through its trespass notices and the extension of appellants’ fall exclusion
period, and (c) such injury will be irreparable in that appellants are unlikely to ever recoup their
losses from the temporary modification of their grazing permits, even if their operations survive.
Consequently, I find that appellants have satisfied this prong of the four-part test in 43 CFR
4.21(b)(1).
Relative Harm to the Parties and
Whether the Public Interest Favors Granting the Stay
Much of what has been said above is relevant to the remaining two prongs of the four-
part test, which in this case entail weighing the harm to appellants against the harms to BLM, the
desert tortoise, and potentially other uses authorized under the CDCA Plan. A stay must be
denied even where there is a likelihood of immediate and irreparable harm to appellants, if the
harm to the opposing party would be greater or if the public interest would be harmed by granting
the stay.
As noted above, Judge Sweitzer’s August 24 decision documents the multiple threats to
the desert tortoise posed by grazing operations, as well as the “near total collapse of tortoise
populations in the Mojave.” ALJ Decision at 29. “The recent severe and catastrophic declines in
desert tortoise populations in California signal a need for new and immediate action to reduce all
sources of mortality and to stabilize populations.” Id. at 24. Moreover, as Judge Sweitzer noted,
Congress in the ESA has afforded listed species “‘the highest of priorities.’ TVA v. Hill,
437 U.S. 153, 174 (1978). Under the ESA, the balance of the hardships has already been struck
in favor of endangered species * * *.” Id. at 76. Indeed, “under the ESA, federally listed species
are to be * * * protected, whatever the cost. [TVA], 437 U.S. at 174, 184.” Id. at 96-97
(emphasis in original).

Of course, like Judge Sweitzer’s statements about economic harm cited previously, these
conclusions were reached in the context of a decision on the merits, not a stay request. It would
certainly be possible to argue that, over the limited duration of a stay, any harm to the desert
tortoise would be much less severe, particularly if the stay included the months between seasonal
exclusion periods. But appellants’ stay requests and motion to IBLA for expedited review sought
to avoid the entire fall 2001 exclusion period, and there is no guarantee that a decision on the
merits of the appeals will be rendered by the start of the spring 2002 exclusion period. Given the
already dire and worsening condition of desert tortoise populations in the Mojave, a stay that
would permit grazing during even one exclusion period would run counter to the public interest
as expressed by Congress in the ESA.
In addition, granting a stay preventing implementation of Stipulation 3 in the Center for
Biological Diversity suit would pose significant risks for BLM and potentially all activities
authorized in the CDCA Plan. Judge Sweitzer described BLM’s decision to negotiate a
settlement of that litigation as follows:
BLM personnel thought the threat of injunction was high, especially for activities
in critical habitat * * *, which is reasonable in light of the § 7(a)(2) mandate to insure that
activities do not adversely modify critical habitat. In sum, BLM reasonably assumed that
an injunction of all activities authorized under the CDCA Plan was likely if it litigated the
Federal court action, and its efforts to reach compromise under such circumstances should
not be discouraged based upon the evidence presented.
ALJ Decision at 65.
In addition to harming the desert tortoise, therefore, a stay in this case could lead the
Center to seek to reopen the litigation in order to prohibit all activities authorized by the CDCA
Plan, pending completion of the lengthy consultation process with FWS. Such a prohibition, of
course, would have far-reaching consequences for BLM, appellant-permittees, the County, and
all users of the CDCA. I therefore find that both the relative harm to the parties and the public
interest militate against granting the stay.
Conclusion
For the foregoing reasons, pursuant to the authority delegated to the Director by 43 CFR
4.5(b), I hereby grant BLM’s petition with respect to appellants Fisher and Mitchell and vacate
IBLA’s October 24, 2001, stay decision with respect to those appellants. All appeals from
